nuggets.summary: Hamilton built his Series A/B fundraising as a deliberate sales funnel rather than a series of ad hoc conversations: he first compiled a list of 70 potential investors, then met with 40 of them at the partner level (not counting associate meetings needed to get there), and then narrowed that pool down to about 6 live offers he could pit against each other for terms. The key sourcing tactic was getting almost all of his intros from other entrepreneurs rather than cold outreach, and deliberately building a network of founders who would each make 2-3 introductions on his behalf. The non-obvious part is treating the number of investor conversations as a volume/practice game — using early meetings to hone the pitch before it mattered — rather than trying to go straight to the few investors he most wanted.
nuggets.quote: the way i approached it was that i needed to learn as much as i could from this process um so i needed to have a real process ... let's find as many investors as possible that might invest in us right ... i had 40 meetings with partners that's not including meetings with all the associates and everybody else to get to the partners i've got almost all my intros from entrepreneurs which is very very important ... the whole idea is to drive as many possible suitors as possible and get down to like you know six offers on the table and then uh then you kind of have your pick of the litter

nuggets.summary: During fundraising, Hamilton controlled exactly how much financial detail different investors saw based on how serious/far-along they were, rather than giving everyone the same pitch deck. Early-stage or less-committed investors got a limited information set; as investors got more serious he progressively revealed more (full P&L, detailed averages); only the firms actually about to sign a term sheet got the fully detailed picture. The logic he gives for holding back until the very end: revealing something after signing exclusivity — even something minor — gives the investor leverage to claim you weren't forthright and use it against you in diligence, whereas showing everything right before signing means they can't later claim they were misled.
nuggets.quote: i manage the information flow very very tightly in terms of i would release this amount of information to the 12 people that are still in and that would reason another amount of information to the seven people that are still in ... when they get down to the end by the by the by the last you know set when people are like ready to put down term sheets you're opening the kimono at that point ... sometimes not being incredibly forthright right before that term sheet can really kill you um because even if the thing is not that big a deal that they didn't know they could use it as a big deal and they can leverage it on you

nuggets.summary: Hamilton argues founders systematically underestimate how much leverage they actually hold over investors, even in a bad-terms scenario after money is raised — the common fear is that a signed deal locks you into whatever the investor wants, but in his view an entrepreneur can always walk away from an unreasonable investor and let the company relationship 'explode,' which is a real cost to the investor too. The practical takeaway is to negotiate hard for clean, simple terms up front (fewer levers for the investor to pull later) rather than assuming you have to accept unfavorable terms just because the money is in the bank.
nuggets.quote: if i mean the entrepreneur can do whatever they want i mean and even in the worst case scenario you got really really terrible terms entrepreneur can stand up and walk out the door and like let the thing explode behind them and you know toss the keys like you can you know so you have much more levers than you think you have

nuggets.summary: Hamilton's biggest cited mistake was a falling-out with Facebook that came from a wrong mental model of the relationship: his team assumed a back-and-forth, collaborative 'partner' dynamic, when in Facebook's eyes TUNE was simply a vendor with no say in how things worked. That mismatch led to friction on calls where his team pushed back as if negotiating with an equal, which from Facebook's side looked like overstepping. The lesson generalizes: before assuming a platform or big-company relationship is a true partnership, explicitly check how the other side actually categorizes you, because a 'vendor' relationship has fundamentally different rules than a 'partner' one, however friendly it feels.
nuggets.quote: we thought that we were partners you know we thought like this partners like we work together we kind of go back and forth on things and stuff like that like actually it's not how they work you're actually a vendor like at all right um and uh and so there are a couple of moments there where like we were on phone calls and i was kind of like what are you talking about we got to do it that way it doesn't even make sense

nuggets.summary: TUNE's stated firing rule inverts the usual instinct to punish the mistake itself: they say they have never fired someone for making a mistake, but have fired people for hiding or not admitting a mistake over an extended period. The underlying test for whether someone is a problem isn't whether they errored, but whether they're self-aware enough to know it — Hamilton gives the concrete diagnostic of a 5-person team where 4 members know someone isn't performing but that person doesn't, calling that specific unawareness-of-reality gap the real red flag requiring a change, not the underperformance itself.
nuggets.quote: we've never fired someone for making a mistake we have fired people for not admitting it for long periods of time right because that's psychotic you know like be aware of yourself and that's that's the main thing that we're looking for and and if there's five members of your team and four of them know that you're not performing but you don't know that's a problem right that's a really big problem you're completely unaware of reality

nuggets.summary: When designing TUNE's culture code (Collaborate, Optimize, Do, Evolve), Hamilton deliberately avoided values that describe subjective traits people could use to attack each other, because vague or judgmental values become 'weapons' in interpersonal conflict rather than genuine behavior guides. Instead the values were chosen to be things that are inherently hard to accuse someone of lacking in a divisive way — closer to baseline professionalism (show up, work well with others) than to trait-based judgments like 'not collaborative enough.' The practical design principle: test a candidate culture value by asking whether it could be weaponized as a personal accusation, not just whether it sounds inspiring.
nuggets.quote: we actually try to pick things that were not really divisive types of things but things that you kind of had to work together on um it's kind of hard to call someone out for like you're not collaborative enough you know uh you know and we just didn't want our values to be like weapons uh that you could really use to hurt each other

nuggets.summary: For post-acquisition integration, Hamilton says the outcome is largely set before the deal even closes: how the acquired team is treated during the deal process itself (respect, ease, even having the acquirer's legal team proactively introduce the incoming people around the company) determines how the team feels about the whole transition afterward. The second concrete integration tactic is getting a key leader from the acquired company connected directly into the executive team and the company's strategic thinking as fast as possible (he cites naming an acquired founder as general manager of TUNE's flagship product), rather than keeping acquired teams siloed under their old identity.
nuggets.quote: it starts with the deal to be honest right like how the deal goes down is going to make a big difference on how the team feels about this deal going down right ... you also really need to do is you need to get them connected up into the executive team as well as you possibly can uh we did that with ian zefferman at mobile dev hq ... him being really connected into the the strategy and the fiber of sort of where the company is going makes a huge huge difference in the ability for that team to adapt and connect to what we're doing

nuggets.summary: Hamilton pushes back on the common startup-hiring dogma that founders must be 'insanely scrutinous' about every hire from day one. He describes TUNE's own early hiring as fast and loose — two interviews and an offer — because at that stage the priority was shipping and filling seats, not perfecting process; only later, once the company had scale and stability, did they slow down and become highly selective. His framing positions himself as more 'practical' than the standard advice, treating early-stage speed-over-precision as a legitimate tradeoff rather than a rookie mistake to avoid.
nuggets.quote: a lot of people say um you know in a startup that you got to just be insanely scrutinous early on sometimes you just need to ship something like sometimes you just need to get it done and i'm okay with that to be honest so i think i might be a little more on the practical side of that

nuggets.summary: Hamilton discloses that TUNE's acquisition track record is roughly 35% successful integration ('batting about 350'), which he frames as better than the average large corporation but still far from perfect — a candid, quantified admission that most acquisitions at any company, including a well-regarded fast-growing startup, don't fully pan out. This is a useful calibration point for founders evaluating their own or others' M&A track record: even a company good at acquiring should expect roughly two-thirds of deals to underperform expectations.
nuggets.quote: so are you batting what 500 about 333 or where you at uh you know i'd give us yeah i mean 350 you know i'd give us about like that

nuggets.summary: On negotiating fundraising terms, Hamilton describes prioritizing clean, simple terms over squeezing the best valuation, explicitly asking his lead investor (Excel Partners) for a 'back of the napkin clean term sheet' and pushing back line by line to strike out the few clauses that gave the investor extra leverage. His stated rationale is that clean terms remove the investor's ability to exert 'weird leverage' later — if there are no special levers in the contract, an investor who starts behaving badly has no real mechanism to force outcomes, which keeps the power dynamic aligned even after the money is in the bank.
nuggets.quote: what we got from excel partners was a uh they sort of call it a back of the napkin clean term sheet right um you know we sat down with the term sheet and there were like two little little things in there they tried to grab from us and we said nope and they crossed that one out ... if you get that right in the deal and you keep the terms really really clean it's gonna be really hard for them to get weird leverage on you

nuggets.summary: Hamilton stakes out a contrarian industry bet that the long-running 'mobile web vs. native app' debate is a false binary that's about to be resolved in apps' favor for navigation, not just engagement. His reasoning: the web wins at navigation but apps win at dwell time/engagement, and the missing piece — a navigation layer for apps analogous to hyperlinks for the web — is already being built via deep linking and app-content indexing (e.g., Spotlight search surfacing specific app pages like a website). He calls people who assume the browser will simply catch up and win 'well-meaning idiots,' arguing that by the time the web catches up on UI, apps will already have superior personalization and context baked in.
nuggets.quote: the question has always been will the web get all the dwell time or will apps get the navigation right and i think we're starting to see the beginnings of the navigation system that will tie the app world together the same way the websites are built together deep linking is the technology that starts this rolling ... you can say the web's going to catch up from a ui perspective um but by the time it does you know apps will be in our brain
